newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh leader warns of gap between rich and poor.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh leader warns of gap between rich and poor.

text.p: Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev stepped back from firing his reformist prime minister on Thursday but warned his government that market reforms could create a dangerous rift between rich and poor.
Nazarbayev had threatened to sack Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin unless he came up with ways to tackle Kazakhstan's dizzying backlog of unpaid wages and pensions.

But presiding like a tough schoolmaster over a government economic meeting, Nazarbayev instead gave his prime minister until the end of the year to pay off debts to pensioners, which now amount to 31 billion tenge ($400 million).
"As I understand your plan, you will start paying pensions regularly from July 1 while all debts will be paid by January 1, 1998," Nazarbayev said.
When Kazhegeldin nodded his assent, Nazarbayev snapped back: "I will be following this personally."
There was no word on unpaid wages. The meeting was watched by reporters on a television link.
A Western economist based in the Kazakh capital Almaty said paying off the arrears under such a timetable was "doable" without printing money.
The government said last month it plans to issue a $200-$250 million yen-denominated Samurai bond this summer to pay debts.

Kazhegeldin said also he planned to raise the budget deficit by half a percentage point above this year's planned 3.16 percent deficit to help meet the arrears. "Any more than that and we risk losing our (credit) rating," he said.
Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan's former Communist Party boss, was seen at the end of last year by diplomats and analysts to be out of touch with the resource-rich republic's economic problems.

But a shrewd operator, Nazarbayev has seized the political initiative by banging government heads together over the payments crisis in an effort to divert popular discontent over the hardships that have followed reform.

Angered by a lack of planning in funding small business in Kazakhstan, Nazarbayev lashed out at his quaking economy minister: "On small and medium business hangs the life or death of reform -- either we create a middle class or we face a dangerous divide between rich and poor."
Amid a hectic privatisation programme in which the country's sickly but reserve-rich oil and gas enterprises are up for sale, Kazakh officials and foreign investors expect an economic boom.
Nazarbayev's technocratic government has moved fast in creating market structures.
But the economic dynamism buzzing in Almaty has passed by much of the 16.9 million population, thrown across a country of bleak steppe land five times the size of France.

With pensions and state wages low even if they are paid, some of the elderly are driven to root through piles of rubbish on the streets of Almaty in search of something to eat, something unheard of in Soviet times.
